title: Minimum Travel Time Through Slow Zones (Dijkstra's Algorithm)
real_world_story: Some parts of the factory floor are slower to cross: a busy packing area, a low-grip surface, or a zone where robots must reduce speed. Moving one cell there costs more seconds than moving one cell down a clear aisle, so the route with the fewest cells is not always the fastest route.

real_world_connection.input_represents: Floor plan where each cell holds the seconds needed to enter it (1 to 9) and -1 marks a blocked machine or storage region
real_world_connection.query_represents: The robot dock cell and the destination cell
real_world_connection.algorithm_represents: Always finalising the currently cheapest reachable cell first, so total time is minimised instead of move count

problem_statement: Given an R x C floor plan where each cell is an integer from 1 to 9 (seconds needed to enter that cell) or -1 (blocked region), a dock cell (sr, sc) and a destination cell (dr, dc), find the minimum total travel time to go from the dock to the destination with 4-directional moves. The entry cost of the dock cell itself is not paid. Blocked cells cannot be entered.
task: Return the minimum total travel time from the dock to the destination, or -1 if the destination cannot be reached.
input_format: The first line contains two integers R and C. The next R lines each contain C integers (1 to 9, or -1 for a blocked cell). The final line contains four integers sr sc dr dc.
output_format: Print the minimum total travel time, or -1 if unreachable. Print 0 when the dock and the destination are the same cell.
constraints: Floor cells are between 1 and 9 (entry cost) or -1 (blocked)
The dock cell and the destination cell are never blocked

examples.explanation: The only route is (0,0) -> (0,1) -> (0,2) -> (1,2) -> (2,2). Paying the entry cost of every cell entered gives 2 + 1 + 3 + 1 = 7 seconds.

The five-move route along the top row enters cells costing 9, 9, 9, 1 and 1, for 29 seconds. The seven-move route that drops to the bottom row and comes back up enters seven cheap cells for 7 seconds, so the longer route is the faster one.

expected_algorithm.name: Dijkstra's Algorithm
expected_algorithm.reason: Cell costs differ, so a level-by-level expansion is not enough. Dijkstra always finalises the cheapest cell still pending and relaxes its neighbours, which gives the minimum total time even when a longer route is cheaper.

hint: Track the cheapest known total time to every cell, starting at the dock with 0.
Always expand the cell with the smallest known total time so far.
When stepping into a cell, add that cell's entry cost to the running total.
real_world_takeaway: When floors, roads or networks have different costs, minimising total cost needs Dijkstra rather than a plain breadth-first search.
